utterances.text: If we could just move on please to paragraphs 32 and 33 of that statement, he goes on to say that "The two bodies in the canyon where the red Opel Kadett was located were recovered with the assistance of the fire brigade who gave us a ladder to get down to the canyon and a rope to haul the body bags with the body inside up to the ground level." Paragraph 33: "The red Opel Kadett had a fire in the trunk which made me think that the two bodies were killed, placed in the trunk of the Opel Kadett and set on fire probably using petrol to set them on fire. The car was then probably pushed into the canyon. A black T-shirt was found in the trunk of the car and the bodies were two to three metres away. The car was on its roof in the canyon when I found it. Later, when the relatives were identifying the car, I think it was then put on its wheels and that's how I later recognised that there had been a fire in the trunk. I remember the family identified the female's ring and her sandals but the male's body was almost 80 per cent burned." Do you see that passage? Now, just bear with me for a moment, if you will, Mr. Dunjic. First of all, as far as the woman's body, R-18, is concerned, do you know whether it was found in the boot of the car, as Mr. Jovovic seems to claim it was found by him and (redacted) in the boot, or whether it was found two to three metres away from the car as (redacted) himself seems to say in his witness statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot be specific about this because I was not a direct participant, so I don't know where the bodies were actually found, whether it was in the trunk or next to the vehicle, although on the photograph of the vehicle that we just looked at, that's R-18, you can see one of the bodies next to the vehicle. But I made this break in order to check another thing, if I may. I will read from an autopsy record regarding an injury found on this woman's body. That's paragraph 8 of the autopsy record. "In the interior part of the right lower leg that has been preserved in the middle third, 26 centimetres above the soles, there is a round hole on the skin about 7 centimetres in diameter, where there is about 1 centimetre of a metal projectile protruding from this defect on the skin. There is no casing on this projectile. When the projectile was extracted and the tissue explored, it was ascertained that the bottom of the defect reaches to the muscle layer through the subcutaneous layer." The reason why I read this is to illustrate a point that this round or projectile had to have been very slow because it did not go through the soft tissue of the leg, which leads one to conclude that it had to have gone through some kind of a solid obstacle on its way, and that the body must have been inside, in an enclosed space, that prevented the round from penetrating deeper into the body. On the basis of what I've just told you a conclusion can be reached that it is highly possible that the body had been in a trunk or inside a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Dunjic, but just pause and think about if you would for a moment the evidence that you've just given. What you seem to be saying to us is that for the bullet not to have travelled through the leg and to have been lodged in the soft tissue, it must have travelled through something else first. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It must have lost the initial momentum that it had, as all the rounds have. In other words, it had to have been going slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just pause for a moment. Two questions on that, if I may. First of all, one of the reasons why a bullet can remain lodged in somebody's soft tissue, and one of the reasons why it may be travelling slowly is because it's been shot from further away, isn't it? The greater the distance, the lesser the velocity of the projectile; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And secondly, Mr. Dunjic, that doesn't help us at all, does it, in understanding whether the body which was burned was inside the boot of the car as a way of concealing it, doesn't help us as to whether a dead body was put into the boot of the car because presumably if your conclusions are correct that the projectiles are associated with the cause of death, then unless you're suggesting somebody was shooting at a dead body, it doesn't help us at all to ascertain whether the dead body was in the boot of the car, does it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about this specific case, in addition to this element, this person had suffered multiple skull fractures. There were also injuries to the cervical part of the spine, and also there were fractures of the left shin bone and of the left upper arm bone. This was not the only injury. In our expert conclusion, we stated, and this is a view that is held by our field of expertise, forensic medicine, that it is very difficult to establish the cause of death in people who are in an advanced degree of decomposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you -- I'm sorry to interrupt you. Did you see the body yourself when you went to the canal on the 11th? So that you can help the Tribunal as to where it was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could you just -- I'm sorry, you're hesitating. Did you or didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was at the canal. I just can't remember whether I actually saw that body but I did see the car that was just below the waterfall, at the very beginning, at the start, of the natural course of the canal, towards Radonjic Lake. So the car was just beneath the waterfall. That was where it was. And you can see that on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's the body that I'm interested in, Mr. Dunjic. If you just look at your witness statement at paragraph 412, can you help us -- could you look at your witness statement at paragraph 412, please?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just finish what I was going to say and then I'll look at it. One body was seen next to the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you -- let me put the question to you again. Did you yourself see the body when you arrived at the canal on the 11th, having refreshed your memory from that statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And where was the body when you saw it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The body that was later labelled as 18 was right next to the canal, but I have to say something which I don't know whether I said in my previous statement or maybe by any of the other witnesses. This car was overturned.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. We understand that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that is how it stood. And this body could be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You could see one body --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, I've just shown you a witness statement made by (redacted) which states that a burned male body was also found two or three metres away from the car. Can you help us with that? Was there a burnt male body found two to three metres away from the car?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now that particular detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Again, when you're looking through the reports overnight, will you see if you can identify for us any 80 per cent burnt male body as described by (redacted)? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could this be printed out for the witness as well, this request?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 421 in your statement, you indicate that the autopsy on this body revealed not just traces of burning but defects from animal teeth inflicted post mortem. Do you see that? Paragraph 421 of your witness statement you indicate there were defects from animal teeth.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And does that indicate scavenging?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Presumably if the body had been found inside the boot of the car, by crime scene technicians, then it couldn't have been scavenged in that way unless it had previously been in the open air for a period of time, could it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot comment on that statement or other statements. I can only tell you what we established in our post mortems. Every injury on the body on a corpse, a dead body, which is bleeding, attracts animals. So I can only assume on the basis of traces of animals. Now, where exactly that body was, was it in the boot and then dragged out of the boot by an animal or was next to the car, what remains as an open issue is caused by the fact that the vehicle overturned and in the course of that overturning, it is quite possible for the body to have fallen out. And then it was accessible to animals or maybe the boot opened up in the course of the tumbling and again it was accessible to animals.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I can entirely understand what you're saying, Mr. Dunjic. The reason I'm asking you is because I've shown you the witness statement of Mr. Jovovic who says that the body was found when he and (redacted) opened the boot. In other words it was found inside a closed boot. If it's got scavenging marks on it, and it was found inside a closed boot, that would mean that it must have been in the open air for some time before going into the boot, sufficient for it to be scavenged, would it not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can be only one possible assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we move into private session for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, one of the people whose names you have recorded in your witness statement has given evidence in these proceedings about being present at Hotel Pastrik during that identification process and has told the Trial Chamber that he has never heard that account that is recorded in paragraph 426 of your witness statement, and that it was never said in his presence by any of his relatives at Hotel Pastrik. Do you see the account that is there recorded, the suggestion at paragraph 426 is that the relatives related the following story about the victim's disappearance. "Ilira was still breast-feeding a baby at the time of her disappearance. KLA members came to Ilira and Tush's home in a hamlet close to Djakovica. They went straight to the victim's home as if it was planned. A relative went to the home and took the baby before Ilira and Tush were taken away by the KLA. I don't recall if the relatives told me that they had" -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "I do not recall if the relatives told me that they had witnessed the kidnappings themselves or if they had heard them described by someone else." Just to repeat, Mr. Dunjic, when this passage of your witness statement was put to the person concerned, he said that he'd never heard any of his relatives suggest that the KLA had kidnapped this couple from their home, that that was not true, and that no one who was present at Hotel Pastrik had said it and that it must be a lie. This is transcript pages 2846 and following. Can you help us with that at all?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. During the process of identification, relatives appeared,

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, please, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For the witness, we return into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break. We'll resume at quarter past 6.00 but return into private session immediately after that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could you turn to paragraph 354 in your witness statement, please? You there make certain references to the physical circumstances in which body R-14 was found. And I'll read into the record the two sentences I want to refer to. You say, "We found the body on September 12 directly next to the concrete wall of the canal. A light layer of pebbles and dirt had covered it by nature rather than man. It was our opinion that rain had caused the earth from the embankment to slide down and cover the body." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just want to be clear, when you say "our opinion," it was obviously the opinion of not just yourself but somebody else. Whose opinion was it apart from yours? With whom did you share that opinion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all three of us, Professor Aleksandric and Dr. Jecmenica. We discussed this. We talked about it. And we reached this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So Professor Aleksandric was party to the conclusion that the layer of pebbles covering body R-14 was a layer of pebbles that had been deposited there by nature rather than by man?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When he testified about this body, Professor Aleksandric told the Trial Chamber that we found bodies 14 and 15 behind the pile of gravel "which could not have ended up naturally there. It could not have been washed up there by the water. It was quite evident that the pile was man-made." Now, I just want to you help us, if you can, please. You tell us that there was a clear discussion between you to the conclusion -- that reached the conclusion that that pile of gravel had arrived there by nature rather than by man. Professor Aleksandric has testified to precisely the reverse effect. Can you shed any light on that at all? This is transcript 6774, line 13.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that area, as you can see on the photographs, there is a quantity of small rocks, and there are some larger rocks there too. What I'm talking about, this thin layer of dirt, the thin layer of dirt and of small gravel, was certainly washed down by the rain from areas further up the slope. The larger rocks and larger gravel found in this area had to have been brought there either up there at the upper levels above the corpse. They were not naturally occurring there in the soil. I think that's what he meant, that that had been brought there by someone. I don't know how it came to be there. But this thin layer of dirt and the small gravel that can be observed on the photographs, it is quite obvious that rain washed down this soil and brought it all the way down to the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you just to look now, please, on another topic at paragraph 97 of your witness statement and I'm going to ask you some questions now about dates of death, estimations that you've given, about dates of death in respect of the remains that you examined or your team examined. Now, paragraph 97, you say that you could not give an accurate estimation of the time of death since the bodies were exposed to various elements and the rate of decomposition is dependent on weather conditions and then you give further explanations in relation to that. May I make it clear to you that in the questions I am about to ask you I am simply concentrating on the remains recorded as having been found at the canal area, that is to say beside the wall or in the canyon, rather than, at this stage, on the remains that are recorded as having been found in and around the economic farm. So I'm asking you questions now about the remains that run from R-1 through to R-35. Without going through it paragraph by paragraph, Mr. Dunjic, you essentially categorise or you and your team essentially categorised the remains into seven categories by age group. You identified three sets of remains as having died sometime in April or May, that's R-12, R-13 and R-14. 11 sets of remains as having died between April and August, two sets of remains as having died between April/May and August, 13 as having died between May and August, one in July or August, one in August, and for two, you provide no date. I want to ask you, against that background, just some questions first of all to help us interpret what you are saying about dates of death. When you say in your statement about any particular body that the appearance of the remains at post mortem were consistent with the death occurring between April and August, does this mean, just for the sake of clarification, that the earliest date that death could have occurred was at any time during the month of April and that the latest date was at any time during the month of August? Is that essentially the parameters that you're setting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In decomposed bodies, a large number of factors affect the appearance of the body and the degree of decomposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment? What Mr. Emmerson is exploring, whether the two dates you gave are the extreme limits or whether there is anything else. He didn't ask you on what basis you do that but his question was, "Do I understand your statement to say that it was not any earlier than April and not any later than August?" That's his question. Would you please focus your answer on that. And then methods might be another question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the two intervals, the broadest possible intervals, April and May. But we cannot be specific whether it was the 1st of April and the 31st of August or another period, but at any rate, this is the period in which these people could have died, could have undergone their fate. So this is the broadest possible interval without being more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so does it follow from that, Mr. Dunjic, that where you say in respect of any particular body that it may have died at any time between April and August, it follows that it could have been an individual who met their death, for example, in the middle of August?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of the bodies that did show signs of putrefaction could have been killed or death could have been caused in the second half of August too or in the first half of August. So it was -- we did not specify the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: For example, we know from other evidence that Serbian forces including paramilitary police, took control of Gllogjan and Rzniq on the 11th and 12th of August. And does it follow from what you told us that where you give a date of April to August inclusive it would be consistent with death having occurred around that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dutertre?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: That was a very general question. If you're talking about a particular body, I imagine the Professor can respond but in such a general question, it's really very vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would say it's not about vagueness. The question includes the answer already. And reading the previous answers of the witness, it's perfectly clear not later than -- not earlier than the 1st of April and not later than the 31st of August includes the 11th or the 12th of August. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we now look, please, at two specific individuals in respect of whom you've given estimations? If we start, please, with R-14, at paragraph 361, you there suggest that in your estimation, based on post mortem findings, that the degree of decomposition for R-14 was consistent with death having occurred possibly in April or May. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And R-15 is the next one. In his case, you at paragraph 371 recorded the more general formulation of April or May to August. Do you see that? This is paragraph 371. Although it does say 1995. Presumably it meant 1998. Do you see that at 371?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. But just so that we are clear, R-15 was originally identified using traditional means as somebody called Milovan Vlahovic. This is 377. But on subsequent analysis, this turned out to be somebody called Istref Krasniqi who is the husband of R-14. So R-14 and R-15 were husband and wife. Do you see? And we've heard evidence that this couple was last seen alive together by relatives in mid-July. I wanted to explore with you briefly, if I could, how and why you felt able to say that R-14 must have died as early as April or May whereas in respect of R-15 you weren't able to give that estimation. I'm trying, if you understand it, to explore the margin of error in your estimates. How were you able to say in respect to R-14 that death must have occurred in April or May?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the degree of decomposition because they weren't identical and if you give a broader time scale, it is possible by applying other possible methods within the scope of investigations to be more specific, so that at the point in time when we were doing this, and observing the bodies, we didn't have a single detail to indicate who the persons were, when they went missing, and under which circumstances. So by giving the broadest possible range on the basis of the level of decomposition, we are trying to assist the investigation, on the one hand, and on the other, the conditions to which the bodies were exposed were different, whether they were on the surface or not, whether they were covered by earth or not, so that we could interpret only what we saw in situ. And on that basis --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand the general approach, Mr. Dunjic. What I'm having difficulty with is in relation to R-14 you didn't give the broadest possible framework. You narrowed it down to April or May. If the position is in fact that that individual was still alive in the middle of July, does that give us some indication of the margin of error in your approach?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you're now mixing up quite a lot of things. If the position is in fact that the individual was still alive in the middle of July has got nothing to do with the margin of error, as a matter of fact. The margin of error is determined only by the methods used and is not influenced by whether a person was according to the testimony still alive at a certain moment. I want you to focus on the additional question because that was a relevant question. Professor Dunjic, Mr. Emmerson was triggered, and let's forget about what other evidence we've heard, that's not primarily for -- at least not at this point in time for Professor Dunjic to consider -- Mr. Emmerson asks how you were able to determine that I think it was R-14, that you could say it was April or May, whereas for R-15, you said it was sometime between April or May and August. So for the period further back in time, you were relatively more specific whereas for a longer period in time, coming closer to the date of the investigation, you are less specific. What made it possible for you to make this distinction in time and period of time on which you said these persons must have died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must point out that this is a framework. It doesn't mean that the body or rather that that person may not have met their death before April or after August. This was the broadest possible frame. As for R-14 and R-15, comparing the two bodies in respect of the degree of putrefaction, my impression was that this person, R-14, the body was decomposed to a greater degree, and that is the reason that I gave this time frame. I cannot be specific and claim this, because this could have occurred also in June or July, but I have endeavoured, on the basis of those changes on the body, to be as precise as possible in setting this time frame, being April or May, which doesn't mean that she could not have met her death later. These are not firm, rigid frameworks, when I say April, May or August. These are not rigid time periods in this case, the decomposition was more advanced so I thought that the person died earlier on, which meant April or May, but I do allow for the possibility as an expert that it could have occurred later. But for the investigation and other examinations that I did not engage in, I just provided a time frame, because for the purpose of further investigative procedures, because we have to provide a time frame for the time of death. And the decomposition found, if they are flagrantly different at the level of skeletalisation, for instance, which requires a longer period of time under certain conditions, then we will say this body could not have met its death in April or May, but it must have been five or six months before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. For R-15, you give a time range of two months. For R-15, you give a time range of-- yes, April, May.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: R-14, it's a time range of April or May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I misspoke. For one of the bodies you give a time range of two months whereas for the other, you give a time range of five months. So what makes you -- what led you to choose a small time range for R-14 and to take a five-month range for R-15? I think that's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of the degree of decomposition and a greater degree of skeletalisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I must admit that I have some difficulties in understanding your answer because if you say the decomposition was further in progress, then I would expect a five-month range, well, let's say from January until May, but not a difference in time range on which you estimate the time when the person died. I mean, you understand what my problem is Mr. Dunjic or not? I do understand that if you say there's further decomposition, then I say, okay, then time of death must have been most likely been earlier. But what I do not understand is why you give a two-month range for April, May, and where you said the person so therefore the decomposition must have been further progressed, whereas at the same time you give a time limit of five months, April and/or May until August for the other body, that's not clear to me. Just in terms of logic and methodology.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The changes that are visible on the body, I'm sorry that we can't see that photograph now of R-14, and the absence of certain bones that are missing, indicate that the body was in the open for a longer period of time. And provisionally, those changes could correspond to persons who went missing in April. We had information that they went missing in April. As for R-15, there was a broader range because in addition to those, to the decomposition, we didn't come across any other changes that could have indicated a longer exposure. So it's possible April to the end of August. In the former case, the decomposition was so pronounced that we thought that that person had died most probably in April or May. That person went missing also. But it is also possible that may have been before April or after May. There is no exact indicator for this. No precise way of saying this person died in April and this one in May. This is on the basis of my own personal experience working on these cases, that these -- the level of decomposition was such that death could have occurred three, four or five months before exhumation or autopsy. For this body, I didn't have any firm evidence, for R-15, but I do allow for the possibility that death may have occurred in April but the tissue was relatively well-preserved so that it is possible that death occurred in August. For an analysis of this kind, in addition to all the indicators found, it is necessary to engage in a comparative analysis of the other bodies found. So it is not possible just to isolate one particular body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, unlike at earlier occasions I'm now looking at the clock. We are five minutes to seven. I'd like to give one statement from the Chamber, which is not related in any way to this witness, which will take me two minutes. I would also like to verify whether Professor Dunjic has been provided or will be provided with the relevant portions of the transcript which allow him to do the homework he accepted to do from the blue binder. Madam Registrar, has the relevant portions been printed out? That's two portions of the transcript. Professor Dunjic, we are close to finishing for the day and at this moment, you are excused. I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have already given or are still about to give, and of course also not to consult anyone on your homework of this evening. The Chamber highly appreciates that you're willing to do this. Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the last time Mr. Dunjic was with us there was a question concerning issues around the analysis of hair and I had requested that any notes or microscopic examinations that the Professor had would be forwarded to the Defence. I spoke with Mr. Dutertre earlier today. He has nothing in his file and I note that Mr. Dunjic has a number of papers with him. I don't know if he's brought any of that information with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can ask him. Mr. Dunjic, the question is that since analysis of hair was discussed earlier, whether there is anything you could assist us with in that respect, that is, whether you have any notes about that, notes either on observations, examinations or perhaps microscopic examinations. Is there anything you have brought today in that respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, Your Honours, we did not engage in any microscopic examinations of hair but only macroscopic examinations during the post mortem and comparisons so that to establish with precision whether the hair came from that particular body, with the noose, I really have no reports about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just want to know whatever you observed in that respect is that concluded in the material which is already available or is there any additional -- are there any additional notes, are there any additional reports on the examination of hair, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't have anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith. I think this answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Professor Dunjic, we would like to see you back tomorrow in the afternoon at quarter past 2.00 in another courtroom, Courtroom III. So therefore when I'm talking about the homework of this evening you even have the morning available which might not be -- okay. So therefore, I'm now asking Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom and we would like to see you back tomorrow. And you can take the blue binder with you and the relevant portions of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would just like to give a statement. If anything happens outside this courtroom which needs to be on the record it will be formally read into the record. The Chamber would like to make a short statement in order to put some of the events from before the recess on the record. On the 10th of July, the Prosecution applied for a videolink for the hearing of one of its witnesses. The statements of this particular witness were subject to a Rule 92 bis application which was pending before the Chamber. On the 11th of July, the Chamber decided to admit the statements of the witness dated the 28th of October 2004 and the 19th of April 2007 as well as the Rule 92 bis attestation pursuant to Rule 92 bis. The Chamber found that there was no need for cross-examination of the witness. The parties were informed about this oral decision through an email from one of the Legal Officers of the Chamber on the 11th of July. The Chamber will give the reasons in its decision on the third batch of Rule 92 bis requests. As a consequence of the Rule 92 bis decision, the Chamber rejected the application for videolink. The parties were informed of this through the same e-mail of the 11th of July 2007. And this concludes the Chamber's statement. Perhaps it needs to check your e-mail but at the same time if decisions are taken, if they are communicated to the parties through e-mails, which is of course not the usual way of communicating decisions, then it should be formally on the record, and as said before, the reasons will find their way in the third 92 bis batch decision. We adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 21st day of August, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.
